source_text: Ἐπεὶ τοίνυν ἀπεδείξαμεν παῖδας ἡμᾶς τοὺς πάντας ὑπὸ τῆς γραφῆς καλουμένους οὐ μόνον, ἀλλὰ καὶ τοὺς Χριστῷ κατηκολουθηκότας ἡμᾶς νηπίους ἀλληγορουμένους, μόνον δὲ εἶναι τέλειον τὸν πατέρα τῶν ὅλων (ἐν αὐτῷ γὰρ ὁ υἱὸς καὶ ἐν τῷ υἱῷ ὁ πατήρ), ὥρα ἡμῖν ἑπομένοις τῇ τάξει καὶ τὸν παιδαγωγὸν ἡμῶν εἰπεῖν ὅστις ἐστί. καλεῖται δὲ Ἰησοῦς. ἔσθ᾿ ὅτε οὖν ποιμένα ἑαυτὸν καλεῖ καὶ λέγει »ἐγώ εἰμι ὁ ποιμὴν ὁ καλός«, κατὰ μεταφορὰν ἀπὸ τῶν ποιμένων τῶν καθηγουμένων τοῖς προβάτοις ὁ καθηγούμενος τῶν παιδίων παιδαγωγὸς νοούμενος, ὁ τῶν νηπίων κηδεμονικὸς ποιμήν· ἁπλοῖ γὰρ οἱ νήπιοι ὡς πρόβατα ἀλληγορούμενοι· »καὶ γενήσονται«, φησίν, »οἱ πάντες μία ποίμνη καὶ εἷς ποιμήν.« παιδαγωγὸς οὖν εἰκότως ὁ λόγος ὁ τοὺς παῖδας ἡμᾶς εἰς σωτηρίαν ἄγων. ἐναργέστατα γοῦν ὁ λόγος περὶ ἑαυτοῦ διὰ Ὠσηὲ εἴρηκεν »ἐγὼ δὲ παιδευτὴς ὑμῶν εἰμι«. παιδαγωγία δὲ ἡ θεοσέβεια, μάθησις οὖσα θεοῦ θεραπείας καὶ παίδευσις εἰς ἐπίγνωσιν ἀληθείας ἀγωγή τε ὀρθὴ ἀνάγουσα εἰς οὐρανόν. Παιδαγωγία δε καλεῖται πολλαχῶς· καὶ γὰρ ἡ τοῦ ἀγομένου καὶ μανθάνοντος, καὶ ἡ τοῦ ἄγοντος καὶ διδάσκοντος, καὶ αὐτὴ τρίτον ἡ ἀγωγή, καὶ τὰ διδασκόμενα τέταρτον, οἷον αἱ ἐντολαί. ἔστι δὲ ἡ κατὰ τὸν θεὸν παιδαγωγία κατευθυσμὸς ἀληθείας εἰς ἐποπτείαν θεοῦ καὶ πράξεων ἁγίων ὑποτύπωσις ἐν αἰωνίῳ διαμονῇ. ὥσπερ οὖν κατευθύνει τὴν φάλαγγα ὁ στρατηγὸς τῆς σωτηρίας τῶν μισθοφόρων προμηθούμενος, καὶ ὡς ὁ κυβερνήτης οἰακίζει τὸ σκάφος σῴζειν προαιρούμενος τοὺς ἐμπλέοντας, οὕτως καὶ ὁ παιδαγωγὸς ἄγει τοὺς παῖδας ἐπὶ τὴν σωτήριον δίαιταν τῆς ἡμῶν αὐτῶν ἕνεκεν κηδεμονίας· καὶ καθόλου ὁπόσα ἂν παρὰ τοῦ θεοῦ εὐλόγως αἰτήσαιμεν ἡμῖν γενέσθαι, ταῦτα πειθομένοις τῷ παιδαγωγῷ περιέσται. ὅνπερ οὖν τρόπον ὁ κυβερνήτης οὐκ αἰεὶ τοῖς ἀνέμοις ὑπείκει, ἀντίπρῳρος δὲ ἔσθ᾿ ὅτε ὅλαις ἀνθίσταται καταιγίσιν, οὕτως ὁ παιδαγωγὸς οὐχὶ τοῖς ἐν τῷ κόσμῳ τῷδε καταπνέουσιν ἀνέμοις ὑπείκει ποτὲ οὐδὲ ἐπιτρέπει αὐτοῖς τὸ παιδίον, ὥσπερ σκάφος, εἰς θηριώδη καὶ ἀσελγῆ προσρῆξαι δίαιταν, μόνῳ δὲ ἄρα τῷ ἀληθείας πνεύματι ἔπουρος ἀρθεὶς ἀντέχεται μάλα ἐρρωμένως τῶν οἰάκων τοῦ παιδός, τῶν ὤτων λέγω, ἕως ἂν ἀβλαβὲς καθορμίσῃ τὸ παιδίον εἰς τὸν λιμένα τῶν οὐρανῶν· τὸ μὲν γὰρ πάτριον καλούμενον παρ᾿ ἀνθρώποις ἔθος ὅσον οὐδέπω παρέρχεται, ἡ δὲ ἀγωγὴ ἡ θεία κτῆμά ἐστιν εἰς ἀεὶ παραμένον. Ἀχιλλέως μὲν οὖν παιδαγωγὸν τὸν Φοίνικά φασι γεγονέναι καὶ τῶν Κροίσου παίδων Ἄδραστον, Ἀλεξάνδρου δὲ Λεωνίδην καὶ Φιλίππου Ναυσίθοον. ἀλλ᾿ ὃ μὲν γυναικομανής, ὁ Φοῖνιξ, ἦν, ὃ δὲ φυγάς, ὁ Ἄδραστος, ἦν, Λεωνίδης δὲ οὐ περιεῖλεν τὸν τῦφον τοῦ Μακεδόνος οὐδὲ Ναυσίθοος μεθύοντα τὸν ἐκ Πέλλης ἰάσατο· Ἀλκιβιάδου δὲ τὴν πορνείαν ὁ Θρᾷξ ἐπισχεῖν οὐκ ἴσχυσεν Ζώπυρος, ἀλλ᾿ ὠνητὸν ἀνδράποδον ὁ Ζώπυρος ἦν, καὶ τῶν Θεμιστοκλέους παίδων ὁ παιδαγωγὸς Σίκιννος οἰκέτης ῥᾴθυμος ἦν· ὀρχεῖσθαί φασιν αὐτὸν καὶ σικιννίζειν εὑρηκέναι. οὐκ ἔλαθον ἡμᾶς οἱ παρὰ Πέρσαις βασίλειοι καλούμενοι παιδαγωγοί, οὓς τέτταρας τὸν ἀριθμὸν ἀριστίνδην ἐκλέγοντες ἐκ πάντων Περσῶν οἱ βασιλεῖς Περσῶν τοῖς σφῶν αὐτῶν ἐφίστων παισίν· ἀλλὰ τοξεύειν μόνον οἱ παῖδες αὐτοῖς μανθάνουσιν, ἡβήσαντες δὲ ἀδελφαῖς καὶ μητράσιν καὶ γυναιξὶν γαμεταῖς τε ἅμα καὶ παλλακίσιν ἀναρίθμοις ἐπιμίσγονται, καθάπερ οἱ κάπροι εἰς συνουσίαν ἠσκημένοι. ὁ δὲ ἡμέτερος παιδαγωγὸς ἅγιος θεὸς Ἰησοῦς, ὁ πάσης τῆς ἀνθρωπότητος καθηγεμὼν λόγος, αὐτὸς ὁ φιλάνθρωπος θεός ἐστι παιδαγωγός. λέγει δέ που διὰ τῆς ᾠδῆς τὸ πνεῦμα τὸ ἅγιον εἰς αὐτόν· »αὐτάρκησεν τὸν λαὸν ἐν τῇ ἐρήμῳ, ἐν δίψει καύματος, ἐν ἀνύδρῳ· ἐκύκλωσεν αὐτὸν καὶ ἐπαίδευσεν αὐτὸν καὶ διεφύλαξεν ὡς κόρην ὀφθαλμοῦ. ὡς ἀετὸς σκεπάσαι νοσσιὰν αὐτοῦ καὶ ἐπὶ τοῖς νεοσσοῖς αὐτοῦ ἐπεπόθησεν. διεὶς τὰς πτέρυγας αὐτοῦ ἐδέξατο αὐτοὺς καὶ ἀνέλαβεν αὐτοὺς ἐπὶ τῶν μεταφρένων αὐτοῦ· κύριος μόνος ἦγεν αὐτοὺς καὶ οὐκ ἦν μετ᾿ αὐτῶν θεὸς ἀλλότριος.« σαφῶς, οἶμαι, τὸν παιδαγωγὸν ἐνδείκνυται ἡ γραφὴ τὴν ἀγωγὴν αὐτοῦ διηγουμένη.
pass_a_gloss: Since, therefore, we have shown that all of us are called children, not only by the scripture, but also that we, who have followed Christ, are called infants allegorically, and that only the Father of all is perfect (for the Son is in Him and the Father is in the Son), it is time for us, following the order, to say who our instructor is. And He is called Jesus. For at times He calls Himself a shepherd and says 'I am the good shepherd', using a metaphor from the shepherds who lead the sheep, the instructor of the children is considered the guardian of the infants, the shepherd who takes care of them; for the infants are simple, like sheep, allegorically. And He says 'and they will all be one flock and one shepherd.' Therefore, the Word is reasonably our instructor, leading us children to salvation. Clearly, the Word has spoken about Himself through Hosea, saying 'I am your instructor.' And the service of God is instruction, being the teaching of the service of God and the guidance to the knowledge of truth, leading uprightly to heaven. Instruction is called by many names: both the one of the person being led and learning, and the one of the person leading and teaching, and the guidance itself, thirdly, and the things being taught, fourthly, such as the commandments. But the instruction according to God is the guidance of truth to the contemplation of God and the imitation of holy deeds in eternal abiding. Just as the general guides the troop, taking care of the salvation of the mercenaries, and as the helmsman steers the ship, intending to save those on board, so also the instructor leads the children to the salvific way of life, for the sake of our own guardianship; and, in general, whatever we might reasonably ask from God to happen to us, these things will be around us, if we obey the instructor. Just as the helmsman does not always yield to the winds, but at times resists all the opposing storms, so also the instructor does not yield to the winds blowing in this world, nor does He allow them to lead the child, like a ship, to a savage and shameless way of life, but, having been raised by the Spirit of truth alone, He strongly holds the helm of the child, that is, the ears, until He moors the child safely in the harbor of heaven; for the paternal custom, so-called among men, is not yet past, but the divine guidance is a possession remaining forever. They say that Achilles' instructor was Phoenix, and that of Croesus' children was Adrastus, and Alexander's was Leonidas, and Philip's was Nausithous. But one was a womanizer, Phoenix, and another was a fugitive, Adrastus, and Leonidas did not restrain the pride of the Macedonian, nor did Nausithous cure the drunkard from Pella; and Zopyrus, the Thracian, was not able to restrain Alcibiades' prostitution, but Zopyrus was a slave for sale, and the instructor of Themistocles' children, Sicinnus, was a lazy servant; they say he invented the sikinnis dance. We have not forgotten the royal instructors among the Persians, whom the kings of Persia, choosing from all Persians, appointed as instructors for their own children; but the children learn from them only to shoot with the bow, and when they come of age, they mingle with their sisters and mothers and wives and countless concubines, like pigs accustomed to intercourse. But our instructor is the holy God Jesus, the Word who leads all humanity, the philanthropic God Himself is the instructor. And the Holy Spirit says somewhere in a song about Him: 'He satisfied the people in the wilderness, in the thirst of heat, in a waterless land; He surrounded them and instructed them and protected them like the apple of His eye. Like an eagle, He covered them with His wings and took care of them, spreading His wings; He took them up on His shoulders and lifted them up; the Lord alone led them, and there was no foreign god with them.' Clearly, the scripture shows the instructor, describing His guidance.
pass_b_english: Since we have demonstrated that Scripture calls all of us children, and that we who follow Christ are allegorically termed infants—while only the Father of all is perfect, because the Son is in Him and the Father is in the Son—it is time, following the logical order, to identify our instructor. His name is Jesus. At times He calls Himself a shepherd and declares, "I am the good shepherd" (John 10:11). By this metaphor, drawn from shepherds who lead their flocks, the One who guides children is understood as a tutor, the guardian shepherd of infants; for infants are simple, like sheep, allegorically speaking. He also says, "And they will become one flock and one shepherd." The Word, then, is rightly our instructor, leading us children to salvation. The Word has spoken very clearly about Himself through Hosea: "I am your instructor." True piety is itself instruction—teaching the service of God and training that brings knowledge of the truth, an upright guidance that leads to heaven. The word 'instruction' is used in several senses: the condition of the one being led and learning, the activity of the one leading and teaching, the guidance itself, and fourth, the things taught, such as the commandments. But instruction that comes from God is the straight guidance of truth toward the contemplation of God and the imitation of holy deeds in eternal abiding. Just as a general directs his phalanx, providing for the salvation of his soldiers, and a helmsman steers his vessel, intending to save those on board, so our instructor leads the children to a salvific way of life out of guardianship for us. In general, whatever good things we might reasonably ask God to grant us, we will obtain them by obeying the instructor. As a helmsman does not always yield to the winds, but sometimes resists head-on the opposing storms, so the instructor never yields to the winds that blow in this world, nor does He allow them to drive the child, like a ship, into a savage and shameless way of life. Rather, lifted by the Spirit of truth alone, He firmly holds the helm of the child—that is, the ears—until He brings the child safely into the harbor of heaven. The so-called paternal custom among men has not yet passed away, but divine instruction is a possession that endures forever. It is said that Achilles' tutor was Phoenix, and Croesus' children had Adrastus, Alexander had Leonidas, and Philip had Nausithous. But Phoenix was a womanizer, Adrastus a fugitive, Leonidas did not restrain the Macedonian's pride, and Nausithous failed to cure the drunkard from Pella. Zopyrus the Thracian could not restrain Alcibiades' prostitution; indeed Zopyrus was a slave for sale. The tutor of Themistocles' children, Sicinnus, was a lazy servant; they say he invented the sikinnis dance. We have not forgotten the royal tutors among the Persians, whom the Persian kings selected as the four best from all Persians and appointed over their own children. Yet those children learn only archery from them, and upon reaching adulthood they cohabit with sisters, mothers, wives, and countless concubines, like boars accustomed to intercourse. But our instructor is the holy God Jesus, the Word who leads all humanity; the philanthropic God Himself is our instructor. The Holy Spirit says somewhere in a song concerning Him: "He satisfied the people in the wilderness, in thirst and heat, in a waterless land; He encircled them, instructed them, and guarded them as the apple of His eye. Like an eagle covering its nest and yearning over its young, He spread His wings, took them up, and bore them on His shoulders; the Lord alone led them, and no foreign god was with them." Clearly, I think, Scripture reveals the instructor by describing His guidance.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the Greek text, including the complex allegorical structure and the historical examples. Scripture citations are handled correctly: Pass B adds the necessary identification (John 10:11) for the quote 'I am the good shepherd', which is required by the instructions for added identifications. The translation of the Hosea/Exodus passage (the song of the Spirit) preserves the imagery and meaning of the Greek.
